analysis.one_liner: Opens more federal land to oil, gas, coal, and mining while speeding permits and limiting environmental review.
analysis.headline: S. 1456 was introduced with 12 Republican cosponsors in May 2023, referred to the Senate Energy Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The SPUR Act would have required the Interior Department to hold quarterly oil and gas lease sales on federal land and approve an offshore leasing plan by a fixed deadline. It would have set a 45-day clock for deciding natural gas export applications — with approval automatic if the deadline was missed — capped environmental reviews for mining projects, made it harder to challenge leases in court, and allowed federal royalty rates on oil from public land to be cut to 12.5 percent. It also would have barred federal mining moratoria, deferred fracking rules to the states, and withdrawn a proposed conservation rule for public land. The bill never moved past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies, coal companies, hardrock mining companies, and LNG export developers. They gain mandated lease sales, potential royalty cuts to 12.5 percent, faster permit decisions, automatic approval of missed export applications, narrower environmental review, and new limits on lawsuits that could delay or cancel leases and mining permits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil, gas, coal, and mining companies

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Interior Department to immediately resume quarterly onshore oil and gas lease sales and conduct a replacement sale within 180 days if any sale is canceled or paused.

Requires approval of a final 2023-2028 offshore leasing program by September 30, 2023, including at least two Gulf of Mexico lease sales per year, and lets the Secretary shorten comment periods to meet the deadline.
Sets a 45-day deadline for final decisions on LNG export applications, with the application deemed approved and its environmental review deemed sufficient if the deadline is missed.

Caps environmental reviews for mining projects at one year for an environmental assessment and two years for an environmental impact statement, and lets a lead agency adopt an environmental document prepared by the mining company itself.

Bars courts from vacating oil and gas leases even when the environmental review behind them violated federal law, instead remanding the issue to the Interior Department while permit processing continues.
Prohibits any federal moratorium on mining leases, claims, or permits on federal land and requires Congress to approve most new federal land withdrawals.
Directs the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to adopt tariff and rate changes to protect the adequacy, affordability, reliability, and security of electricity and interstate natural gas delivery.
Bars the Interior Secretary from enforcing federal fracking rules on federal land in states that have their own fracking regulations.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers collect less from oil produced on public land because the bill lets royalty rates drop to 12.5 percent. People living near drilling, mining, and pipeline routes get weaker environmental review and fewer ways to challenge projects in court. Households bear the downstream costs of expanded fossil fuel production, including pollution and climate damage, and conservation of public land gets a lower priority.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and communities near drilling and mining

drawbacks.text: The Secretary may cut federal oil and gas royalty rates to as little as 12.5 percent for five years, reducing the revenue taxpayers receive for resources taken from public land.
Decisions on LNG export applications are automatically approved if the Energy Department misses the 45-day deadline, removing a checkpoint even where the review was incomplete.
Bars the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission from considering upstream or downstream greenhouse gas emissions or any social cost metric when reviewing natural gas pipelines and transmission lines.

Lawsuits over lease sales must be filed within 60 days, courts cannot vacate leases found to rest on unlawful environmental reviews, and mining permit challenges face a 60-day bar and a requirement to show imminent and substantial environmental harm before any pause.
Withdraws the Bureau of Land Management's proposed Conservation and Landscape Health rule and extends grazing permit renewal terms, reducing the department's tools for managing rangeland.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that the bill goes beyond speeding clean reviews: it mandates more leasing, lowers the price industry pays for public minerals, and narrows public and judicial oversight rather than simply making agencies faster.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real, narrower case inside this bill — energy projects can take years to permit, and faster, more coordinated reviews can lower costs without weakening protections. But most of the bill is not streamlining. It mandates quarterly lease sales and coal lease offerings, cuts royalty rates toward the minimum, deems export applications approved when deadlines slip, and closes off court challenges even where the underlying review broke the law. The public gives up revenue and oversight for uncertain supply benefits, and the balance comes out clearly on the cost side.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee in May 2023, and the committee never took it up, so it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator John Barrasso introduced the SPUR Act on May 4, 2023, joined by 12 Republican cosponsors, all in the Senate minority.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no committee report, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people and the federal treasury came out ahead in the narrow sense that the bill never advanced: royalty rates on public oil stayed where they were, environmental review and court oversight of leases and mining permits were unchanged, and no new offshore leasing plan was forced on a shortened clock. The energy, coal, and mining industries that the bill was written for did not get the expanded access it promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public; the bill never advanced

industries.note: The bill mandates quarterly onshore lease sales and annual Gulf of Mexico sales, lets royalties fall to 12.5 percent, and shields leases from court challenges even when reviews broke the law. Companies profit from more public land and lower payments while the public absorbs lower revenue and environmental risk.

The bill bars federal mining moratoria, caps reviews at one to two years, lets agencies adopt company-prepared environmental documents, and makes it much harder for courts to pause a permit. Mining gains access and speed; nearby communities lose a say.

A 45-day decision deadline with automatic approval on delay, and small-scale exports deemed automatically in the public interest, speed up facilities whose main product is sold abroad. The public gets the siting impacts and narrower review.

The bill requires quarterly coal lease offerings and declares an existing environmental assessment sufficient to resume new federal coal leases, restarting a paused program on terms favorable to lessees.

FERC is directed to adopt tariffs protecting the affordability and reliability of gas delivery, and reviews of gas projects must ignore upstream and downstream emissions. The bill entrenches pipelines' role while removing climate considerations from their approval.
